1226.title: Simplify, simplify
1226.hook: our life is frittered away by detail: simplify, simplify (Walden 2)
1226.howItsDone: Some readers of Walden take 'simplify, simplify' as a working practice, trimming one routine or possession at a time to make room for what they count as essential.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cabin's cost: a receipt to the half cent, and a thing's true price in life. Your line was what it cost.

How many small decisions has today asked for so far? Which shirt. Which reply. Which of four reminders first. Each one tiny, none worth a second thought. And yet by evening, a day like that can seem used up, though it's hard to say on what. Thoreau had a word for this, long before inboxes. In the second chapter of Walden, on where he lived and what he lived for, he calls it frittering. And he answers it with one word, said again and again.
screen: `SO MANY TINY CHOICES.` → `THE DAY USED UP.` → `ONE WORD, REPEATED.`

segments.voice: First, the diagnosis: "Our life is frittered away by detail." Frittered is an exact word. Not stolen. Not wasted in one big mistake. Crumbled away in small pieces, the way a cookie disappears in crumbs. Second, the cry: "Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!" Three times, with an exclamation mark. An honest person, he says, hardly needs to count past their ten fingers, in extreme cases adding the ten toes, and lumping the rest. He's joking, and he means it: keep your affairs few enough to count on your hands. Third, the instruction: simplify. The word turns from a quality into a verb. Simplicity is something you admire; simplify is something you do. His examples are deliberately blunt: fewer meals, if one will do, fewer dishes, and the rest reduced in proportion. The point isn't the menu. Simplifying happens in specific, ordinary places, not in general. Fourth, simple isn't empty. This is the chapter where Thoreau explains why he went to the woods at all, to live deliberately, as day ninety-one put it. Clearing the clutter was never the goal. It made room for what he called the essential, so that something could finally get his full attention. So the question isn't just what can I drop. It's what am I clearing space for.
screen: `FRITTERED AWAY BY DETAIL.` · `SIMPLICITY, THREE TIMES.` · `SIMPLIFY IS A VERB.` · `CLEARING ROOM FOR SOMETHING.` · then, large: `SIMPLIFY.`

segments.voice: Pick one ordinary routine, getting ready in the morning, making dinner, the first hour at work, and walk through it in your mind, step by step. Notice the small steps that crumble the time: the extra checking, the choosing, the things done only out of habit. Now picture the same routine with one step gone, just one, and feel how it is to move through it lighter.
Simplify. Thoreau's answer in Walden to a life frittered away by detail: keep your affairs few enough to count on your fingers, and clear room for what's essential. Today's word.

1227.title: Reading the classics
1227.hook: read the best books first, or you may not get to them (Walden 3)
1227.howItsDone: Some readers of Walden keep one demanding book close at hand and read a little of it slowly each day, in the spirit of Thoreau's chapter on reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simplify: a life frittered away by detail, and room cleared for the essential. Your line was simplify.

A stack by the bed. A great book someone meant to finish, the bookmark stalled near the start. On top of it, the phone, which is easier to pick up. Thoreau lived in a one-room cabin with very little furniture, and yet the third chapter of Walden isn't about saws or beans. It's called Reading. And in his earlier river book, he left advice that sounds simple and stings a little: read the best books first, or you may never get to them at all.
screen: `THE STACK BY THE BED.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED READING.` → `THE BEST BOOKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the order of things. The best books first is a line about time. Life is short, and reading hours are few. Fill them with whatever's nearest, and the great things wait forever. It's yesterday's simplify, applied to a bookshelf. Second, how to read: "Books must be read as deliberately and reservedly as they were written." Slowly, with attention, one considered sentence at a time. He compares real reading to a kind of exercise, something that asks you to stand on tiptoe, not something to doze over. Third, the book on the table. Thoreau tells us he kept Homer's Iliad on his table through the summer at the pond, and looked at it only now and then, because there was a house to finish and beans to hoe. The great book sat there, and he didn't read it as much as he meant to. That honesty is part of the lesson. Even Thoreau had a stack. Fourth, what a book can do: "How many a man has dated a new era in his life from the reading of a book." A whole new era, starting from a page. Not every book does that, but you can't know which one will unless you open it. That's the reason for the best books first: not to be impressive, but so the book that might change your life gets its chance.

1228.title: The bloom of the present
1228.hook: some mornings he sat in his doorway from sunrise to noon, unwilling to trade the moment for work (Walden 4)
1228.howItsDone: Some readers of Walden keep unhurried time in a doorway, on a porch or by a window, after Thoreau's mornings sitting from sunrise to noon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the classics, and the Iliad sitting half-read on Thoreau's table. Your line was the best books first.

A summer morning at the pond. Thoreau has had his swim. He sits down in the sunny doorway of his cabin, among the pines and hickories, and he stays there. The sun climbs. Birds sing around him and pass through the house. A wagon rattles on the distant road. He doesn't get up, not at nine, not at ten: sunrise to noon, he tells us, on some mornings. Somewhere in Concord, a neighbor is already halfway through the day's work. And Thoreau, in the fourth chapter of Walden, says he couldn't afford to do otherwise.
screen: `A SUNNY DOORWAY.` → `SUNRISE TO NOON.` → `HE COULDN'T AFFORD TO MOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the strange economics: "There were times when I could not afford to sacrifice the bloom of the present moment to any work, whether of the head or hands." Could not afford. He uses money language on purpose. The man who printed the cost of his cabin now says some mornings were too valuable to spend on work. Second, the bloom. A bloom doesn't last. It opens, it's at its best, and then it's gone, whether anyone looks or not. The present moment, he suggests, has a bloom like that, and work of any kind, even good thinking, can trade it away. Third, the margin: "I love a broad margin to my life." A page with wide margins isn't wasteful. It's easier to read, with room for notes and for breath. He wanted a life laid out like that. He says he grew in those seasons like corn in the night. You don't watch corn grow; it happens while nothing seems to be happening. Fourth, the honest objection. To his neighbors, he says, it would have seemed like idleness. He doesn't argue much. He simply reports that those hours were not time subtracted from his life but added to it. You don't have to agree. But it's worth asking when you last let a moment bloom without trying to use it for anything.
screen: `COULD NOT AFFORD TO WORK.` · `A BLOOM DOESN'T LAST.` · `A BROAD MARGIN.` · `IDLENESS, OR GROWTH?` · then, large: `THE BLOOM OF THE PRESENT.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit near a door or a window, somewhere with a little outside in it; if not, wherever you are is fine. Let your hands go still, with nothing to plan or review, nothing to be used for anything. Let whatever is here, light, a sound, the temperature of the air, simply open in front of you, like something blooming that doesn't need you to do a thing.
The bloom of the present. Thoreau's phrase in Walden for the moment at its best, which he would not sacrifice to any work, of head or hands, on certain mornings in his doorway. Today's word.

1229.title: The sounds of Walden
1229.hook: the train whistle, the owl, the bullfrogs: Walden's sounds (Walden 4)
1229.howItsDone: Some readers of Walden practice sitting still outdoors and naming what they hear, after the Sounds chapter, including the noises of roads and trains as well as birds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bloom of the present: a doorway, sunrise to noon, and a broad margin to a life. Your line was the bloom of the present.

A scream across the treetops, like a hawk over a farmyard. Then a rumble, and the railroad cars roll past the far edge of the pond. Later, church bells from distant towns, softened by miles of woods. At dusk, a whip-poor-will. At night, owls. And from the water's edge, a deep, absurd croaking that carries on into the night. It's easy to assume Thoreau went to the woods for silence. But the chapter right after Reading is called Sounds, and it's full of noise.
screen: `A SCREAM LIKE A HAWK.` → `BELLS, OWLS, FROGS.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: First, a second kind of reading. Sounds begins by turning from books. If you read only written languages, Thoreau warns, you may forget "the language which all things and events speak without metaphor." The world is also a text, and listening is how you read it. Second, the train. He doesn't pretend the railroad isn't there. The whistle cuts through his woods summer and winter, and he's half annoyed, half thrilled. He watches the cars carry goods from far away, and notices townspeople setting their clocks by them. The modern world is part of the soundscape, and he listens to it too. Third, the bells and the birds. On some Sundays he could hear church bells from several towns. Crossing the woods, the sound changed, as if the pine needles on the horizon were the strings of a harp and the bell had swept across them. The distance made its own music. Then the evening birds: whip-poor-wills, and owls whose cries he calls mournful and strange, and which he's glad are there. Fourth, the frogs. Late at night, the bullfrogs take over the pond, trumping to each other across the water. Thoreau writes their croak down as a long, rolling sound, and clearly enjoys them. Nothing here is holy in the usual sense. That's the point. Close attention turns a train, an owl and a frog into a kind of reading.

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and listen the way Thoreau listened from his doorway: find one sound and name it plainly, a fan, a car, a bird, your own breath, then a second, until you have five. Some will be near and some far, some pleasant and some not. Don't sort them into good and bad; let each one be part of the place you're in.
The sounds of Walden. Thoreau's chapter of listening: the train whistle, distant bells, owls, bullfrogs, and what he calls the language all things and events speak without metaphor. Today's word.

1230.title: Companionable solitude
1230.hook: I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude (Walden 5)
1230.howItsDone: Some readers of Walden set aside regular time alone, walking or sitting quietly, and treat it as company rather than as loneliness, after the Solitude chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sounds of Walden: a train whistle, bells through the pines, bullfrogs trumping in the dark. Your line was sounds.

A rainy evening. No visitors. The nearest neighbor is a long walk away. For some people, that's a picture of loneliness. For Thoreau, in the fifth chapter of Walden, it's something close to good company. He calls the chapter Solitude, and he says, without apology, that he enjoyed being alone. More than that: solitude was the best companion he'd found. Some readers find that sentence beautiful, and others find it a little suspicious. It's worth listening to carefully.
screen: `A RAINY EVENING, ALONE.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED SOLITUDE.` → `THE BEST COMPANION.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence: "I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude." Companion and companionable, side by side, on purpose. In this line, solitude isn't the absence of company. It is company, and of a good kind. Second, the surprise: "We are for the most part more lonely when we go abroad among men than when we stay in our chambers." Loneliness, he suggests, isn't about how many people are near. You can feel it at a crowded party and be free of it in an empty room. Solitude, he says, isn't measured in the miles between people. Third, the rain. Thoreau is honest that it wasn't always easy. Early on, for an hour, he wondered whether he needed people nearby to live well. Then, in a gentle rain, he felt suddenly aware of a sweet and kindly society in nature itself, in the pattering of the drops and every sound around his house. The loneliness passed and didn't return. Fourth, the joke: "I have a great deal of company in my house; especially in the morning, when nobody calls." It's funny, and exact. When nobody calls, there's room for the morning, the pond and his own thoughts. His solitude was never total: he walked into town, and friends came by. But being alone, for him, was something to be glad of, not something to be cured.

segments.voice: For these two minutes nobody needs anything from you, and you don't need anything from anybody; notice what it's like to be your own company, restful or restless, either is fine. Then see if you can treat yourself the way Thoreau treated the rain, as company worth keeping. Let there be a little warmth toward the one who is sitting here.

1231.title: Three chairs
1231.hook: I had three chairs in my house: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society (Walden 6)
1231.howItsDone: Some readers of Walden use the three chairs as a check on how their time is shared between being alone, time with one friend, and time with larger groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday, companionable solitude: a rainy evening, and company found in the pattering of the drops. Your line was companionable solitude.

Three chairs. That's how a man known for living alone counts the seats in his small cabin. After a chapter praising solitude, Thoreau opens the very next one, Visitors, by saying he thinks he loves society as much as most. Then he tells us how his house was arranged for it, in one plain sentence: "I had three chairs in my house; one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society."
screen: `AFTER SOLITUDE, VISITORS.` → `HE LOVED SOCIETY TOO.` → `THREE CHAIRS.`

segments.voice: First, one chair. Solitude gets its own seat, and it comes first: that's yesterday's lesson, sitting quietly in the corner. Second, two chairs. Friendship needs exactly one more: two people facing each other, close enough to hear without raising a voice. Some of life's real conversations happen like this, across a kitchen table, in the front seats of a car, on a bench. Not in a crowd. Third, three chairs. Society, the wider world, still gets a place. When more visitors came than he had chairs for, they stood, and he tells us with some pride how many people his small room could hold. A cabin, he suggests, is roomier than it looks when the guests are good company. Fourth, the room big thoughts need. Here's a lovely complaint: "One inconvenience I sometimes experienced in so small a house, the difficulty of getting to a sufficient distance from my guest when we began to utter the big thoughts in big words." Big ideas, he says, need space to settle, like a bullet needing room to straighten its flight, so he and a friend would push their chairs back and back until they touched opposite walls. It's a joke, and it isn't. Some conversations need distance. Others need closeness. Three chairs is a quiet map of a whole life: room to be alone, room for one friend, and room for the world.

1232.title: The bean field
1232.hook: he hoed beans to know beans, and to learn patience (Walden 7)
1232.howItsDone: Readers of Walden often take the bean field as a picture of slow, attentive work: tending something by hand until you know it, and accepting that what you grow is shared with more than you.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three chairs: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society. Your line was three chairs.

Early morning, a field near a pond, and a man with a hoe. The rows are long, the weeds are quick, and something keeps nibbling the young leaves overnight. He works through the dew until the sun gets high, then goes in. Tomorrow, the same. A neighbor passing on the road might see nothing but a farmer's job, and not a very efficient one. Thoreau saw something else. He gave this field a whole chapter of Walden, called The Bean-Field, and in it he says he was determined to know beans.
screen: `A MAN WITH A HOE.` → `ROW AFTER ROW.` → `DETERMINED TO KNOW BEANS.`

segments.voice: First, the work itself. Thoreau describes his daily labor as making the earth "say beans instead of grass." It's a funny line, and an honest one. The ground wanted to grow its own things; every morning he asked it to grow his. Second, the question he can't quite answer. Why raise beans at all? He doesn't give a tidy reason. He grew to love his rows, he says, though there were more of them than he needed. The love came from the doing, not from a plan. Third, the joke inside the title. In plain American speech, someone who doesn't know beans doesn't know much. Thoreau turns it around: he spent a summer bent over one plant because he wanted to know beans, really know them, the way you only know something you've tended with your own hands. Some people, he says, must work in fields so that a parable-maker will one day have words to use. He was farming and writing the parable at the same time. Fourth, the patience. Beans don't hurry, and the field is never only yours. He names his enemies plainly: "worms, cool days, and most of all woodchucks." But by the end of the chapter he softens. He wonders whether the beans grow partly for the woodchucks, and writes, "These beans have results which are not harvested by me." The patience he learned wasn't just waiting. It was letting the field belong to more than him.
screen: `SAY BEANS INSTEAD OF GRASS.` · `WHY RAISE THEM AT ALL?` · `DETERMINED TO KNOW BEANS.` · then, large: `THE WOODCHUCKS' SHARE.`

segments.voice: Turn toward a plant near you, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, a tree outside the window, or bring to mind one you've known, and look at it the way a person looks at something they mean to know: one leaf, its edge, where it's growing toward. Notice that it's in no hurry at all. If you can, give it one small thing, a little water or a dead leaf removed, and then let it be.
